text: You already know what a resource group and a VNet are, and you already created them with the Azure CLI in the Azure Administration course. This lesson writes the same two objects as a real Terraform configuration — declarative resource blocks instead of two imperative commands you'd have to remember to re-run in the right order.

azurerm_resource_group takes just a name and a location. azurerm_virtual_network takes address_space as a list, even with one CIDR block, because a VNet can technically hold more than one range, plus location and resource_group_name — and here those two aren't typed in literally as strings, they're read straight off the resource group above with azurerm_resource_group.example.location and azurerm_resource_group.example.name.

Nothing attaches to a VNet directly — everything attaches to a subnet, exactly as the Azure Administration course taught. azurerm_subnet is its own resource type, and virtual_network_name references the parent VNet by its name string, not by a generated ID the way you'll see AWS do it next lesson. address_prefixes is a list for the same reason address_space was: usually one entry, but the schema allows more.

Nowhere in this file does anything say 'create the resource group first, then the VNet, then the subnets.' Terraform works that order out on its own, purely from the references: the VNet literally cannot know the resource group's location until the resource group exists, so Terraform's dependency graph creates it first, then the VNet, then both subnets — four resources, three implicit edges, zero explicit ordering written by hand.

This is what terraform plan actually prints for this exact file before a single Azure API call fires: four resources, every one marked for creation, summarized as Plan: 4 to add, 0 to change, 0 to destroy. The order they're listed in here is incidental — what really governs the order apply executes in is the dependency graph underneath, not the order resources appear in the plan output or the file.

Next lesson builds the AWS equivalent of this exact network — a VPC and two subnets, sized with the same CIDR blocks — using the real aws provider. The resource names change, and so does the way resources reference each other: AWS leans on generated IDs where azurerm just leaned on plain name strings.
